abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: We characterize the transcriptomic and morphological dynamics of enteric neurons emerging in the chick embryo gastrointestinal tract. Neurons elongating their projections express axon guidance gene programs that differ from those that guide the colonization of their progenitors of origin, the enteric vagal neural crest cells. These programs also show differences between emerging neuron types, suggesting that they are part of the mechanisms directing the morphological diversity of the enteric neurons and the patterning of stereotypic circuits. Cross-species analyses show that the logic governing early subtype emergence and axon guidance processes is conserved between chick, mice, and humans. They also identify conserved subtype-specific axon guidance genes, including ISLR2, which we show, contribute to the formation of chick enteric axon patterns.

sec.p: Keywords: embryonic development, chick embryo, enteric nervous system, neural crest, axon guidance

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The genetic programs directing nascent enteric nervous circuits and their unique architecture remain poorly characterized. To gain insight, we combined manipulations in the chick embryo model, whole gut three-dimensional (3D) imaging, and single-nucleus transcriptomics at very short intervals for time-resolved analyses of neuronal subtype trajectories. In imaging, we found highly dynamic axon network growth, with rapid increase in axon density and spatial orientation diversification. At transcriptomic levels, we correlated these changes to cell-state transitions with specific axon guidance gene sets. Cross-analyses with human and mouse embryo scRNAseq and expression profiles revealed globally conserved enteric lineage trajectories and subtypes specific axon guidance programs in all species. Finally, manipulation of DSCAM and ISLR2 evolutionary conserved networks in chick whole gut cultures altered enteric axon patterns, validating our paradigm and its applicability to advance current knowledge on human enteric circuit wiring.

sec.p: Received 2025 May 7; Accepted 2026 May 21; Issue date 2026 Jul 14.

body.p: The architecture of neuronal circuits is highly diverse and is essential for the specific functions they ensure. The enteric nervous system (ENS) has unique architecture, conserved across vertebrates. The hundred million neurons composing the ENS encompass a diversity of subtypes that form repeated ganglia distributed within two plexi (myenteric and submucosal) and interconnected by axon networks. They control many aspects of gastrointestinal physiology from its motility, nutrient absorption to satiety. They also contribute to the intestinal barrier protective role, undoubtedly having many other key and yet still unknown roles. The best correlation between the ENS architecture and its function is the regulation of bolus progression. First, the sensory neurons detect the bolus and relay the information to interneurons. Second, the resulting stimulation is propagated in both upstream and downstream directions, to excitatory and to inhibitory motoneurons, respectively. Third, the coordinated upstream contraction of smooth muscles and downstream relaxation propels the bolus forward (1, 2).

This process is intimately dependent on the topographic organization of the circuit along the three axes of the gastrointestinal tract. Accordingly, radially oriented axons from sensory neurons contact the luminal epithelium, axons from interneurons are longitudinally oriented in both rostro-caudal directions, while axons from motoneurons innervating the inner muscle layer have a circumferential orientation (1–7).

The correct ENS architecture depends on a complex developmental sequence. Enteric cells arise from the vagal and sacral neural crests (ENCCs). These cells migrate over large distances and populate the entire GI tract during embryonic development. ENCCs give rise to the diversity of glial cells and neuron subtypes (8–10) under the control of transcriptomic programs that have been closely investigated by single cell transcriptomic (scRNA-seq) in the recent years (11–20). In contrast, very little is known about the subsequent steps during which axon subtypes differentiate and navigate within the developing GI to build the circuit architecture. Consequently, the outcome of alteration of these processes remains unclear. So far, pediatric GI motility disorders are attributed to failure of ENCCs to colonize some GI regions resulting in aganglionosis (10, 21, 22). This is well documented in Hirschsprung disease, which is caused by aganglionosis of the distal colon. Intriguingly, aganglionic part resection does not always restore normal GI Motility (10, 23, 24). The underlying causes, that include miswiring of ENS circuits in GI regions colonized by ENCCs, are still debated. Advancing our knowledge of the mechanisms that direct axon differentiation and the establishment of the circuit architecture could bring novel etiological hypotheses for these diseases.

Here we investigate the early steps of axon development using as a model the chick embryo that has provided seminal contributions to our current understanding of ENS development (25–27). Despite specificities like the presence of gizzard, the general architecture of the ENS in two plexi and their morphogenesis is conserved between chick, mice, and humans (26, 27). The accurate staging of embryonic development makes the chick a model of choice for investigating the fast dynamic of axon pathfinding, Moreover, this model is particularly well-suited for investigating ENS architecture in 3D and visualizing individual morphologies with mosaic neuronal labeling produced by in ovo electroporation of fluorescent reporter in the vagal neural crest. Finally, its well-annotated genome enables in-depth scRNA-seq transcriptomic approaches (12, 28).

We characterize the developmental sequence of enteric axons and show how the axon network acquires complexity over time, both in terms of amount and trajectory and in terms of the diversity of neuron types that emerge from the division of neural crest progenitors. We show the correlated dynamics of axon guidance transcriptomic programs and identify specific signatures to the various differentiating neuron types. Finally, we validate at the protein level the expression of two guidance receptors of these signatures, own Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule (DSCAM) and ISRL2, whose variants are found in children suffering from gastrointestinal dysmotility, and show in whole intestine cultures that they contribute to the formation of correct enteric axon patterns. Comparisons between chick, mouse, and human transcriptomic data support a conservation of early enteric neuron differentiation and identify genes coding for axon guidance receptors and cell adhesion molecules that exhibit similar subtype-specific expressions in all three species. Taken together, our study provides insights into the mechanisms that govern the formation of enteric circuits and opens up perspectives in the context of enteric childhood diseases.

sec.title: Early Steps of Neuronal Differentiation and Axon Development in the Chick Embryo.
sec.p: To study the axonal morphologies of differentiating enteric neurons in the chick embryo, we focused on a preumbilical intestine (p-UI) segment lying between the gizzard and the yolk sac (umbilicus), which is populated by NCC-derived neurons at early stages (25, 29–31) (Fig. 1A). In this region, neurons were reported to start their specification at E4.5 (30, 31) and to form a complex network of interconnected ganglia by E8 (29). We therefore selected E4 to E7 as window of time for our study.

sec.p: First, in whole mount gut, we performed immunolabeling of the neuronal specification marker ELAVL3-4 (HuC/D) and of the neuron specific beta3 tubulin (Tuj1), which labels both the soma and their processes. HuC/D and Tuj1 labeling confirmed that at E4 neurons are already specified in p-UI and have extended processes at E4. We observed a clear rostro-caudal gradient of differentiation correlating ENCC gut colonization, with neurons at the front, close to the umbilicus, that already started axon differentiation (Fig. 1 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S1 A and B). Thus, as reported in mice (32, 33), axon differentiation occurs near the ENCC migration front. As development progresses, we observed an axon network complexification, with an increase of the Tuj1 positive surface between E4, E5, E6, and E7 and of neuron clustering, visible at E7 (Fig. 1 B and C).

We quantified HuC/D staining and found that neuron density only slightly increased from E4 to E5 but increased by 5.3-fold between E5 and E6 and 1.8-fold between E6 to E7 (Fig. 1B). To estimate the specific growth of processes, we subtracted the Hu-positive soma labeling from that of Tuj1 and found that the surface occupied by neuronal processes increased by more than 3.7-fold between E4 and E5, continuing to rise up until E7 (SI Appendix, Fig. S1C). Using Neurofilament staining we could confirm that many Tuj1 processes were axons up to the yolk stalk (SI Appendix, Fig. S1D). HUC/D and Tuj1 labeling, showed that enteric neurons of the p-UI are only present in the outer layers of the developing gut at E5 and E6, beginning to populate the inner layers at E7 (SI Appendix, Fig. S1E). Neuronal differentiation in this region may start in the myenteric plexus, as in other species and consistently with other studies in chick (30, 34).

sec.title: Single Nucleus RNA-Seq Captures Neuron Diversity of Early Developing Enteric Nervous System in the Chick Embryo.
sec.p: To correlate our characterization of neuron and axon development with genetic programs, we performed single-nuclei RNA-seq (snRNA-seq), reported particularly suited to neurons (35), on whole p-UI from E5, E6, and E7 embryos, as data for this region and stages were lacking (12, 28). Unsupervised clustering of the integrated datasets identified the different cell populations of the p-UI gut sample (Fig. 2A). ENCCs and neurons formed clusters, readily identified by specific expression of the ENS marker, RET, also detected by hybridization chain reaction fluorescent in situ (HCR RNA-FISH) in many cells covering the p-UI (Fig. 2B and SI Appendix, Fig. S2A) (26, 36). Consistently with our imaging, we found that the fraction of ENS cells relative to the total gut cells gradually increased between E5 and E7 (E5 5.27%, E6 8.6%, E7 15.05%).

sec.p: Next, to characterize the different neuron subtypes, we subsetted ENCCs and neurons (8,528 cells). Consistently with a neuronal differentiation from an ENCC pool (SOX10+), uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) representations showed that ENCCs and neurons (ELAV4+ and GAP43+) form distinct clusters interconnected by a neuroblast cluster (ELAV4+, ASCL1+, GAP43−) (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Fig. S2B). As expected, using our validated protocol of dual HCR RNA-FISH (37), we found in the p-UI that cells expressing SOX10 and NEFM, a specific neuron differentiation marker, lie close to each other but are distinct (SI Appendix, Fig. S2C). We also identified a small individual neuronal cluster expressing high level of NEFM and ISL1, corresponding to the ganglionic chain of the Remak nerve, a nerve structure lost in mammals (30) (Fig. 2C).

ENCCs, neuroblasts, and neurons were subdivided into several clusters that we identified with gene markers reporting ENS development in other species (11, 15, 17–19) (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Fig. S2 D–G and Table S1). We distinguished cycling from noncycling ENCCs, neuroblasts, glial and bipotent progenitors based on FABP7 and ELAVL4 expression. Markers of terminal differentiation of glia (S100B, GFAP, DHH) were absent, yet one cluster expressed markers of the early step of glial differentiation (PMP22, NRP3), suggesting that some ENCCs are committed to glial fate before E7 (SI Appendix, Fig. S2F). Consistently with a start of differentiation of glia at these stages, we found in E10 publicly available chick dataset, cells expressing some glial terminal differentiation markers (12, 38) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2H). In UMAP representations, enteric neurons distributed into two branches depicting two distinct sublineages specifically expressing the ETS variant transcription factor 1 (ETV1) or the Basocuclin 2 (BNC2) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2I), similarly to other species (11, 15, 19). The ETV1 branch was composed of 3 clusters (ETV1.1, ETV1.2, ETV1.3) while BNC2 branch consisted of a single cluster (BNC2) (Fig. 2C).

Next, we analyzed the dynamics of the ENS clusters between E5 and E7. Both integrated data and individual timepoints showed a progressive differentiation of glial progenitors, with the emergence of a committed glial fate at E6 (Fig. 2 D and E). These analyses also supported an increasing diversification of neurons. We found that ETV1 neurons differentiate before BNC2 neurons, that mainly appear at E6 (Fig. 2 D and E). HCR RNA-FISH confirmed this sequence (Fig. 2F). Interestingly, individual timepoints analysis suggests a gradual emergence of different BNC2 subtypes. Indeed, two BNC2 clusters were identified at E7 (Fig. 2E). Annotation transfer showed that the BNC2 cluster at E6 contains neurons resembling both BNC2 subtypes present at E7 (Fig. 2G). We also observed changes among the ETV1 clusters, with increasing ETV1.3 neuron proportion between E5 and E7 in the integrated data (Fig. 2D and SI Appendix, Fig. S2J). Individual timepoint analysis suggested that transcriptomic differences rise among ETV1 neurons between E5 and E7 since the same clustering parameters resolve two clusters at E5 but three at E6 and E7 (Fig. 2E). Yet, detailed analysis and reference-based annotations demonstrated that the ETV1.1, ETV1.2, and ETV1.3 neurons at E7 are present from E5 (Fig. 2G and SI Appendix, Fig. S2K) and that the proportion of the ETV1.3 neurons among ETV1 neurons increases from 17% at E5 to 36% at E7 as observed in the integrated data.

Next, we further characterized the different immature neuron clusters. We found they share several neuronal markers (GAP43, TUBB3, STMN2, NEFM), and also express specific markers, the top ones including transcription factors and genes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis (Fig. 2H and SI Appendix, Fig. S2 F and L–O). As observed in other species (15), immature ETV1 neurons segregated into nitrergic (ETV1.1) and cholinergic neurons (ETV1.3) (Fig. 2H). HCR RNA-FISH confirmed that some ETV1 neurons express NOS1 (nitric oxide synthase 1) and that NOS1 expressing neurons are distinct from VACHT (Vesicular Acetylcholine Transporter, SLC18A3) (Fig. 2I). Despite potential neurotransmitter developmental switches, neurotransmitter codes generally characterize neuron subtypes (3, 8, 12, 15, 39–41). Thus, ETV1.1, ETV1.2, and ETV1.3 and BNC2 clusters might represent different neuron subtypes.

Next, we investigated the conservation of the chick early enteric neuron differentiation by analyzing published scRNA-seq data from mice and humans. Developmental stage correspondences between the different species have been established based on the timing of gut colonization by ENCCs. Accordingly, E5 to E7 stages in chick would correspond to E10.5 to E13.5–E14.5 in mice and week 4 to 7 in humans (28, 34). Analysis of human week 6 to 11 data from Elmentaite and collaborators (11) showed that enteric neuron diversification occurs before glia differentiation that is only observed at later stage (10 wk of development) and confirmed the presence of two neuronal clusters in the BNC2 expressing branch and three in the one expressing ETV1 (Fig. 2J and SI Appendix, Fig. S3 A–C). Similarly, in mice, we found that differentiated glia is absent and that neuronal clusters distribute into two branches at E12.5 and E14.5 (Fig. 2L and SI Appendix, Fig. S3 D and E). Moreover, beyond UMAPs resemblance (Fig. 2 C, J, and L), we found that chick neuronal clusters share gene markers with human and mouse ones (Fig. 2H and SI Appendix, Fig. S3 C, E, and F). Yet, few markers exhibited differences between the three species. GAL was enriched in ETV1 branch in mice but was expressed in both branches in humans and in BNC2 in chick (SI Appendix, Fig. S3G). CPNE8 that labels human BNC2, was rather expressed in ETV1.3 in both chick and mice (SI Appendix, Fig. S3H). TAC1 labeled both humans and chick ETV1.3, whereas in mice it was expressed by BNC2 clusters (Fig. 2H and SI Appendix, Fig. S3 C and E).

Next, to better assess transcriptomic similarities between humans or mice and chicken, we applied a label transfer approach. Human and mouse data were modified to keep only genes having chick orthologues and neuronal clusters were redefined (SI Appendix, Supporting Information Text SI Material and Methods). Human cluster labels onto chick showed that the chick ETV1.1 cluster matches the human ETV1.1, chick ETV1.2 and ETV1.3 with the human mix ETV1.2&ETV1.3 cluster, while the BNC2 cluster matches the human BNC2.1 cluster (Fig. 2K and SI Appendix, Fig. S3I). The transfer of initial annotations (SI Appendix, Supporting Information Text SI Material and Methods) consistently showed that A1 and A2 annotations are predominant in chick ETV1.1 and ETV1.2 cluster respectively and that A3 is only present in chick ETV1.3 (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 J–L). In addition, cells from the BNC2 chick cluster may not only relate to the human B1 but also to the B2 identity, that is mostly found in the human BNC2.2 cluster (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 K–M). Even though cluster and initial annotations slightly differ (SI Appendix, Fig. S3M), both label transfers show that chick neuronal subpopulations exhibit transcriptomic similarities to human ones. Yet, all chick clusters also contained small proportions of cells having unexpected predicted identities (Fig. 2K and SI Appendix, Fig. S3L). Similarly to humans, label transfer indicated transcriptomic resemblances between chick and mouse ETV1.1, ETV1.2/3, and BNC2 clusters (Fig. 2M and SI Appendix, Fig. S3N). As with the human initial annotation, label transfer identified two populations within the chick BNC2 cluster, one similar to mouse BNC2.1 and the other to mouse BNC2.2 (Fig. 2M). These analyses revealed transcriptional similarities between chick and mouse and human neuronal clusters and suggest that they correspond to different immature subtypes.

While human A1, B1, and B2 clusters are considered to generate motoneurons and A2 and A3 IPANs and interneurons (11), how mouse E12.5–E14.5 subpopulations relate to mature subtypes is not known. To better understand this, we performed annotation transfer of the neuron clusters identified in mouse E15.5 data (15) onto the mouse E12.5–E14.5 ones (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 O–Q). We found that early ETV1.1 cluster comprises both E15.5 ETV1.1 and ETV1.2 identities. The ETV1.3 cluster at E12.5–E14.5 relates to the ETV1.3 cluster in E15.5 data (Fig. 2N). In contrast, we found no clear correspondence for the early ETV1.2 cluster. Finally, we found that one of the two early BNC2 clusters relates to BNC2.1 and BNC2.2 clusters, while the second one relates to BNC2.2, BNC2.3, and BNC2.4 at E15.5 (Fig. 2N). According to published annotations of E15.5 neurons with postnatal identities (15), early mouse ETV1.1 neurons relate to ENC8 and ENC9 (inhibitory motoneurons), mETV1.3 to ENC12 (IPANs), mBNC2.1 to ENC1-3 (excitatory motoneurons), and mBNC2.2 to mix of ENC3 (excitatory motoneurons) and ENC5-7 (interneurons and nonconventional IPAN).

Overall, these different comparative analyses suggest that chick ETV1.1 neurons are committed to inhibitory motoneurons, ETV1.2 and ETV1.3 to interneurons and IPANs, and BNC2 to excitatory motoneurons.

sec.title: SnRNA-Seq Identifies Axon Guidance Gene Programs of Early Differentiating Enteric Neurons.
sec.p: Increase of axonal complexity observed in the E5 to E7 time window might be reflected in enteric neuron gene programs. Consistently, GSEA analysis first showed that several gene ontology (GO) pathways such as “neuronal projection development” (NES:1.73, p-adjusted: 3.7 × 10−5) are enriched in neurons, compared to ENCCs (Fig. 3A). Interestingly, 50% of the top genes are axon guidance receptors or ligands although the referenced axon guidance pathway (GO 0007411) showed no significant GSEA enrichment (NES: 1.21, p-adjusted: 0.15) (Fig. 3B). This might reflect its use by both migrating ENCCs and differentiating neurons (19, 42–44) but also possibly gene set composition. We found that the chick axon guidance gene set lacks 177 genes present in the human equivalent pathway (Fig. 3C), although avian orthologues exist for 146 of them (82%) in our dataset. We found that the human set also lacks several receptors and ligands with known axon guidance functions. Finally, for both species, these gene sets include transcription factors and intracellular effectors generally downstream of several axon guidance signaling (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A and Dataset S1).

(A and B) GSEA plots for the genes of the “neuron projection development” biological pathway (A) and of the chick axon guidance pathway (B). (C) Venn diagram showing gene numbers in the chick and human axon guidance GO gene sets. (D) Venn diagram of the receptor genes in the gene set of the GO human axon guidance pathway and in the homemade list. (E) GSEA plot of the homemade list of axon guidance receptors. (F) Volcano plot showing the distribution of the axon guidance receptors differentially expressed between neuron and ENCCs clusters. (G) Circle plots showing the intercellular communication networks between neurons and other gut cell-types. Left and Right plots show the aggregate weight of the CellChat inferred interactions for secreted ligand and cell–cell contact signaling, respectively. (H) Chord diagrams showing the ligand–receptor interactions for SEMA3, WNT, and SLIT pathways between gut cells and ENCCs (Left) and neurons (Right).

sec.p: Thus, to get a more comprehensive view of the enteric neuron communication, we built a list restricted to receptors and cell adhesion molecules, based on the literature (SI Appendix, Table S2 and Supporting Information Text SI Materials and Methods). Compared to the GO gene sets, it comprises additional receptors and cell adhesion molecules (88 for humans and 130 for chick) (Fig. 3D, SI Appendix, Fig. S4B, and Dataset S2). We found that 99% (159/160) of the listed genes are present in our snRNA-seq data, with 106 genes expressed in more than 5% of the neurons (Dataset S3). In GSEA analysis, the homemade list was significantly enriched in neurons, compared to ENCCs (NES:1.76, p-adjusted: 8.24 × 10−5, Fig. 3E and Dataset S4). We found 57 axon guidance receptors and cell adhesion molecules upregulated in neurons, among which CELSR3 having reported enteric axon guidance role in mice (45) (FC > 1.3, p-adjusted < 0.01), 49 of which are expressed in more than 5% of the neurons (Fig. 3F and Dataset S5). In mirror, 47 axon guidance receptor gene transcripts were selectively enriched in ENCCs, among which the well-known regulator of enteric ENCC migration, EDNRB, and also Frizzled receptors, suggesting an activity of the WNT pathway (Fig. 3F and Dataset S5). We also found activity of Slit and class 3 Semaphorin signaling in both ENCC and neurons, with specificity arising from differential receptor expression by each cell type (Fig. 3F).

Next, we conducted a cell–cell communication inference analysis with CellChat package (46). Although 70 receptors of our list were missing, it revealed a diversity of interactions, with neurons communicating together and with ENCCs, reports and non-ENS sources, consistent with previous reports (Fig. 3G) (33, 47). It also confirmed that ENCCs and enteric neurons have distinct communication pathways and use of SLIT and class 3 semaphorin signaling (Fig. 3H and SI Appendix, Fig. S4 C and D).

sec.title: Complexification of Axon Trajectories Correlates with Increased Diversity of Neuron-Types Having Specific Guidance Signatures.
sec.p: Mature enteric neuron subtypes have stereotypical morphologies and axon orientations (3–5, 7). In mice, the first axons are longitudinally oriented (32, 33, 45), axons with circumferential orientations coming shortly after (48, 49). To characterize the dynamics of axon trajectories at individual cell levels, we expressed by electroporation a cytoplasmic GFP reporter in premigratory vagal NCCs, which resulted in many labeled cells in the developing gut up to the umbilicus (Fig. 4A). We performed light sheet imaging of p-UI in whole mount embryos counterstained with neurofilament (NEFM) at E4, E5, and E6 (Fig. 4B). We applied filament tracer (Imaris) methodology to capture neuron 3D morphologies and found that a majority were unipolar, extending axons in various directions (Fig. 4C, SI Appendix, Fig. S5 A and C, and Movie S1).

sec.p: We measured the angle between the axon axis and the longitudinal edge of the intestine (Fig. 4D). We found that the proportion of longitudinally oriented axons dropped between E4 and E5 from 79 to 45%. Conversely, circumferential trajectories progressively increased over time, reaching 55% at E5 (Fig. 4E and SI Appendix, Fig. S5D). At E6, the axon network density prevented trajectory quantification. Thus, such diversification of axon trajectories correlated with the emergence of new enteric neuron cell types within the E4-E7 time window (SI Appendix, Fig. S5E).

We then studied the dynamics of axon guidance receptor and cell adhesion molecule programs over time to identify topographic signaling that would direct the various axon trajectories. We performed a differential gene expression analysis between neurons at E5, E6, and E7. 29 genes of the homemade list were regulated, increasing in majority (19 genes) (FC > 1.25, p-adjusted < 0.05, pct1 > 0.1) (Fig. 4F). This could either reflect ongoing global neuronal differentiation or alternatively, newly emerging neuron subtypes. Focusing on the top 10 temporally upregulated receptor genes, nine appeared specifically enriched in one of the two neuronal clusters (ETV1.3 and BNC2) that increased between E5 and E7 (Fig. 4F and SI Appendix, Fig. S6 A and B).

We then analyzed the relative expression of axon guidance receptor/cell adhesion molecule genes in the different neuron clusters (Fig. 4G). DGE analysis showed that 57 out of the 160 transcripts were differentially expressed (Dataset S6). Focusing on genes having the strongest foldchange and fraction ratio, we found combinations of both cluster-specific and overlapping genes expressed in different neuronal clusters. Likewise, DSCAM and EFNA5 were restricted to the related ETV1.2 and ETV1.3 clusters while BMPR1B was only expressed in the ETV1.3 cluster. MET transcript was detected in the ETV1.2 cluster, while GFRA2 and PLXNA2 transcripts were detected in the BNC2 cluster (Fig. 4G). Then, by combining up-regulated and downregulated axon guidance genes we could generate cluster-specific signatures (Fig. 4H and SI Appendix, Table S3), thus suggesting that the diversity of axon trajectories correlates with axon guidance gene programs linked to neuron identity.

Next, we studied the temporal dynamic of these signatures (Fig. 4I). We found rather limited cluster-specific temporal regulation of axon receptor gene expressions (FC > 1.25, p-adjusted < 0.05, pct1 > 0.1), although some changes over time were suggested by the dot plots (SI Appendix, Fig. S6C). The observed changes were contrasted between clusters. For ETV1.1 and BNC2 clusters, changes exclusively concerned non-cluster-specific genes, apart for 1, suggesting rather stable specific axon guidance gene programs (Fig. 4J). In contrast, for ETV1.2 and ETV1.3 clusters, 3 out of 4 regulated genes were cluster-specific, likely reflecting emerging new neuron-types (Fig. 4J).

sec.title: ISLR2 and DSCAM Are Expressed in Axon Forming Neurons and Could Engage Multiple Interactions.
sec.p: Next, to functionally test our bioinformatic predictions, we selected two candidates highly upregulated during the ENCC to neuron transition, highly enriched in specific subclusters, and expressed from E5, a stage enabling analyses of axon morphologies, in at least 30% of the neurons (SI Appendix, Fig. S6C). ISLR2 and DSCAM met these criteria, expressed in NEFM positive neurons (37% of NEFM positive cells are DSCAM positive and 72% are ISLR2 positive). ISLR2 (Immunoglobulin Superfamily Containing Leucine-rich Repeat 2), also known as Linx, is critical for central and peripheral axons in different species (50–53). DSCAM is a cell adhesion molecule with a well-known role in axon guidance, that regulates gut innervation in drosophila (54–61). First, we studied the expression profile of their interactome. To compensate for the lack of data in chick, we compiled the physical interactions with plasma membrane and secreted proteins having chick homologs, reported in different species. The ISLR2 interactome comprises VASORIN (VASN) ligand and membrane receptors such as RET, NTRK1, ROBO1. The DSCAM interactome includes cell adhesion molecules like NCAM and ligands like Slits and Netrins (Fig. 5A and Dataset S7). Transcripts for several interactors were found expressed in diverse cell-types of the gut tissue in our snRNAseq datasets (Fig. 5 B and C). We ran CellChat analysis with a customized database that includes DSCAM and ISLR2 interactors, which predicted various interactions (Fig. 5D and SI Appendix, Fig. S6D).

sec.p: We observed by HCR RNA-FISH in whole mount embryos that ISLR2 and DSCAM are expressed in the NEFM-positive neuron population of the p-UI, at E5 and E6. Their patterns however differed (DSCAM: 30% at E5 of NEFM+ and 50% at E6; ISLR2 77% at E5 and 78% at E6), which is consistent with their expression in our snRNAseq data (SI Appendix, Fig. S6 E–G). Next, to observe individual cells within the network and study their morphology, we performed in ovo electroporation of vagal ENCCs with GFP. Then, we identified within GFP positive cells those expressing ISLR2 by FISH and their axons by NEFM immunolabeling (Fig. 5E and SI Appendix, Fig. S5B). We traced the morphology of 49 neurons. Interestingly, within the axon network, 69% of ISLR2 positive neurons had longitudinally oriented axons, a proportion significantly enriched when compared to the total GFP positive population (45%) (Chi2, P = 0.0006) (Fig. 5E and SI Appendix, Fig. S5D). To investigate whether orientation specificity is supported by ISLR2 expression in enteric neurons, we analyzed ISRL2 expression in NFEM positive cells at E5. Interestingly, at this stage, the majority of NEFM positive neurons expressing high ISLR2 levels (60%) belongs to ETV1.2 and ETV1.3 clusters, with only a small proportion (7.7%) coexpressing the motoneuron marker NOS1 (SI Appendix, Fig. S6H). This suggests that ISLR2 may be restricted to a specific neuronal subpopulation that forms longitudinally oriented axons at E5.

sec.title: Conserved and Species-Specific Transcriptomic Programs Direct Axon Development.
sec.p: Next, we studied the interspecies conservation of axon guidance programs. First, we analyzed these programs in ENCCs and neurons in mouse and human scRNAseq. We found significant changes during ENCC to neuron transition in both species, as in chick (Fig. 6 A and B). Then, we focused on genes upregulated in neurons (FC > 1.3, P < 0.05, Dataset S8). We found that 74% of these genes in mice (37/50 at E12.5–E14.5 and 43/58 at E15.5) and 66% of those in humans (25/38) were also enriched in chick neurons (Fig. 6C and SI Appendix, Fig. S7 A and B). 22 of these genes, coding for receptors and cell adhesion molecules including NCAM2, CELRS3, and also DSCAM and ISLR2, were common (SI Appendix, Table S4). This reflected consistent conservation, given relative mismatch between stages.

sec.p: Second, we applied the chick signatures to mouse and human neurons but found that they did not discriminate the different neuronal clusters. Thus, we performed differential gene expression (DGE) analysis of human and mouse neuron-types (FC > 1.3, P < 0.05, pct1 > 0.15). Despite low gene number in humans, likely due to weaker detection, we observed for both species that neuronal clusters express specific axon guidance receptors/cell adhesion molecules, as in chick (E12.5–E14.5 and E15.5) (Fig. 6 D and E, SI Appendix, Fig. S7 C and D, and Dataset S9).

Third, we identified communalities between matched chick–mouse–human individual clusters (Fig. 6F and SI Appendix, Fig. S7 E–G and Table S4). They reached 47% when comparing chick and mouse ETV1.3 cluster and dropped to 17% for the less defined ETV1.2 clusters (Fig. 6F). In human–chick comparison, 15% genes for ETV1.2 and 60% for BNC2 were common. Common genes included BMPR1B, PCDH7, CNTN1 in ETV1.3, GFRA2, and RET in ETV1.1 and GFRA2, ROBO2 in BNC2 (SI Appendix, Table S4). We also compared in mice the E12.5–E14.5 and E15.5 stages and found that dynamic regulation over time, as in chick. For all clusters except ETV1.3, up to 42% of the genes at E12.5–E14.5 were absent at E15.5. For ETV1.3, all genes at E12.5–E14.5 were found upregulated at E15.5 (SI Appendix, Fig. S7 G–I).

Interestingly, high DSCAM and ISLR2 enrichment in neurons was common to all three species (Fig. 6 A and B). Notably, while we observed some interspecies distribution differences for DSCAM, ISLR2 pattern was common and restricted to the ETV1 branch neurons (Fig. 6G and SI Appendix, Figs. S6G and S7 J and K). Moreover, we found several genes of the ISLR2 interactor network expressed within the large landscape of human gut tissue, supporting its activity (SI Appendix, Fig. S7L). Consistently, ISLR2 immunolabeling in slices of human fetus intestine samples revealed strong expression in neurons of both plexi (Fig. 6H). By whole gut immunolabeling of 8- and 12-wk samples, we observed that ISLR2 is mainly expressed in longitudinal axons (Fig. 6 I and J). Some radial axons projecting toward the intestinal villi were also visible in 12 wk cross-sections (Fig. 6J).

sec.title: ISLR2 and DSCAM Contribute to Chick Enteric Axon Development.
sec.p: To explore ISLR2 and DSCAM roles, we took advantage of ex vivo whole gut cultures, proven useful to study ENS development (62, 63). E4 guts were pinned in silicone-lined dish and cultured for 24 h. We analyzed neuron differentiation and process formation with measures of Tuj1-positive cell surfaces. We found the network significantly increased, when compared to E4, becoming comparable to that at E5, thus validating proper ex vivo axon differentiation (SI Appendix, Fig. S7M). Next, we manipulated ISLR2 and DSCAM signaling. We incubated whole gut cultures with either soluble VASN, whose interaction with ISLR2 is well characterized and functional (53, 64) or with soluble DSCAM, its physiologically shedded ectodomain shown to regulate retinal axon development (56, 65).

We compared Tuj1 positive cell surfaces of treated guts and controls incubated with Immunoglobulin Fc fragment (FC). We found that addition of DSCAM and VASN increased the Tuj1-positive surface by 1.78-fold and 1.95-fold respectively (FC-control protein: 8.03 ± 1.16, N = 16; DSCAM: 16.20 ± 2.43, N = 16; VASN: 14.81 ± 2.68, N = 15) (Fig. 6K). Interestingly, the number of differentiating neurons remained comparable, suggesting that ISLR2 and DSCAM primarily impacted on axonal processes (FC: 18.7 ± 2.37, N = 9; DSCAM: 24.8 ± 2.76, N = 10; VASN: 24.6 ± 2.76, N = 12, FC vs. DSCAM P = 0.089; FC vs. VASN; P = 0.152, Mann–Whitney).

Next, we adapted a qualitative guidance index that we previously developed to assess axon orientation in 3D cultures, consisting in blind ranking of a reference region lying closed to yolk sac (umbilicus), with an index from 1 (all longitudinal) to −1 (all circumferential) (66). We found that DSCAM and VASN modified the stereotypical axon patterns by decreasing the longitudinally oriented axon fraction (FC: 0.41 ± 0.12, N = 22; DSCAM: −0.05 ± 0.13, N = 21; VASN: −0.08 ± 0.08, N = 23) (Fig. 6L). This suggests that the DSCAM and ISLR2 interactomes could contribute to axon guidance during ENS axon development.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Guidance decisions are directed by cell-type specific ligand–receptor interactions, in close coupling with cell adhesion molecule dynamics (67–69). To characterize the principles that regulate the pathfinding of enteric axon subsets, a first necessary step was to understand the temporal dynamics of enteric neuron generation and cell identity allocation.

sec.title: Conserved Developmental Logic of Enteric Neuron Generation and Diversification.
sec.p: Our analyses revealed that the developmental trajectories follow similar general rules in chick, mice, and humans. First, we found that the temporal sequence of enteric neuron generation first and glial cells second, reported in mice and humans (11, 15, 19), is conserved in chick. Second, we found that the generation of enteric neuron-types was also conserved. Immature neurons organize in two branches characterized by the specific expression of ETV1 and BNC2. This revealed an evolutionary conserved early binary fate choice from zebrafish to mice and humans (11, 14, 15). Third, we found that neurons can be further subdivided into several clusters that exhibit an ordered sequence of generation over time. Our cross-species analysis indicates that neurons present in chick BNC2 and ETV1 neurons exhibit transcriptional similarities with their mouse and human counterparts. Beyond, we also found species specificities, with some genes being expressed differently in humans and depending on the cases, in either chick and/or mice.

sec.title: Switch of Axon Guidance Programs during the ENCC to Neuron Transition and Neuron Differentiation.
sec.p: We found that the transition from ENCC to neuron is associated with profound transcriptional changes that are also reflected in their axon guidance receptor repertoires. Thus, although exposed to common environment, both ENCCs and neurons activate specific axon guidance mechanisms. The ENCC axon guidance gene signature is consistent with the literature, for example containing ENDRB predicted to be ENCC specific (42).

Conversely, we observed several upregulated guidance receptor genes in enteric neurons compared to ENCCs, suggesting they gain responsiveness to guidance cues, likely reflecting increased complexity of guidance decisions underlying the diversity of axon trajectories. Our CellChat analysis predicts a range of ligand–receptor interactions mediating the communication of enteric neurons with cell-types of the developing gut. Significant neuron–neuron communications are also predicted, mediated by genes having both broad and restricted expression among the neuronal population. For example, UNC5C and NCAM1 are expressed in most neurons, and may mediate common processes. In contrast, DSCAM, TRK3, MET, GFRA2, and BMPR1B have much restricted expression, and may contribute to subtype-specific guidance decisions. Consistently with a conservation of the general program of neuronal specification, we found that many genes of these signatures were also enriched in mouse and human neurons, including CELSR3, a known regulator of axon development (45) as well as those we focused on, ISLR2 and DSCAM.

sec.title: Dynamics of Enteric Axon Patterns and Axon Guidance Gene Programs.
sec.p: Over a 3-d window, we observed two distinct phases. First, neuronal processes extend from a relatively stable number of neurons. Second, the neuronal population strikingly expands, which is accompanied by a significant increase in the axonal network. In addition, we observed a diversification of axonal trajectories with longitudinal orientation dominating in the first phase and circumferential and oblique orientations appearing in the second. Interestingly, this temporal change in axon orientation is consistent with observations in mice, supporting it is an important and conserved principle of ENS circuit development (8, 32, 33, 45, 47–49). Correlation of these observations with data from snRNAseq supports that the increasing diversity of axon trajectories over time results from newly differentiating neuron-types choosing trajectories that differ from previous ones. Consistently, we observed the emergence of neuron clusters with distinct axon guidance signatures in all species, which may direct the selection of specific axon trajectories.

It is, however, difficult to correlate cell identity, axon trajectory, and axon guidance gene signatures. Axon trajectories during development usually prefigure the future axon position of mature neurons. Thus, early orientation might be inferred from mature neuron morphologies, extensively studied for most cell-types (3, 5, 7, 15). Interneurons, for example, have longitudinally oriented axons that may result from an initial longitudinal trajectory. In contrast, motoneurons have more complex morphology, with an initial axon segment longitudinally oriented and long circumferential axonal branches. Their axons could therefore orient initially longitudinally before specifically extending circumferentially (5, 7). Thus, although having very distinct axon morphologies, the axons of these two cell-types may initially share a common longitudinal orientation.

Whether axon guidance genes are part of the identity programs of enteric neurons or rather reflect axon orientation regardless of their identity remains unclear. Our bioinformatic analysis shows that neurons that will later on acquire distinct identities cluster together at the time of early axon differentiation and share cluster-specific axon guidance signatures. They cannot be bioinformatically subdivided according to their future identity, which thus makes the definition of identity-specific axon guidance gene signatures challenging. Interestingly nevertheless, we observed that within the cluster-specific signatures, genes label only subsets of cells. Moreover, they are not all coexpressed in individual cells, which argues that more specific gene combinations may translate already existing heterogeneous cell identities.

Closer investigation of ISLR2, exclusively expressed in the ETV1 branch but at different levels in clusters that could give rise to motoneurons and interneurons, provides some insights. Unexpectedly from these identities, we observed that ISLR2-positive neurons exclusively extend longitudinal axons. However, our quantification of the neurons expressing high level of ISRL2 suggests that the imaged ISLR2 positive neurons might mainly be interneurons, consistent with their observed longitudinal axon orientation.

Our functional ex vivo studies suggest that ISLR2 and DSCAM networks contribute to the formation of enteric axon patterns, although the key interactions within their network remain unclear. Interestingly, and consistent with the longitudinal axon orientation of ISLR2-positive neurons, manipulating ISLR2 resulted in decrease of longitudinal trajectories. This functional approach paves the way to future closer investigations of the axon guidance gene programs directing the formation of enteric axon patterns.

sec.title: Identification of Axon Guidance Genes Relevant to Mouse and Human ENS Physio-Pathology.
sec.p: Beyond interspecies differences and technical limitations of the comparisons (SI Appendix, Supplemental Information Text), we found that the expression of several receptors and cell adhesion molecules was consistently enriched in chick, mouse, and human equivalent neuronal clusters. Interestingly, alterations of ENS were reported in deficient mouse models for several of them, including GFRA1, GFRA2, NTRK3, CNTN1, or BMP signaling (70–75). Some of these alterations could be attributable to abnormal axon network formation.

Moreover, human genetic studies suggest that several genes with conserved expression are relevant to human enteric nervous system (ENS) development. Variants of the GFRA2 ligand NRTN, BMPs, and NTRK3 are associated with Hirschsprung disease (HD) (76–81). Similarly, SEMA3A signaling has been shown to be altered in HD patients (82). Interestingly, variants were identified for DSCAM in some HD patients, and for ISLR2 in children with abdominal distension (83–85).

The reported functions of these genes during axon differentiation support the possibility that pathogenic consequences on gastrointestinal motility may arise not only from developmental changes in the composition and proportion of neuronal subtypes, but also from changes in enteric axon patterns, as suggested for HD (45, 86). This calls for a detailed investigation of the molecular programs that control the formation of enteric axon patterns. Our identification of neuron type-specific markers, including some that distribute in the axons, should help to resolve the diversity of axon subpopulations, allowing their individual monitoring and facilitating their characterization in patient samples.

Finally, our findings extend the relevance of the chick embryo, already acknowledged as an insightful model to explore ENCC migration (25–27), to studies of enteric neuron differentiation and of physio-pathologically relevant genes.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: Detailed materials and methods are provided in SI Appendix, Supporting Information Text. Briefly, experiments with chick embryos and human samples were achieved according to ethical legislation. In ovo electroporation of vagal ENCCs was performed on E1.5 chick embryos (HH9). Ex vivo gut culture was adapted from ref. 63. HCR RNA-FISH, immunolabeling, and light sheet imaging was performed as in ref. 37. Images were processed with Imaris 9.0.2 and 10.0.1 (Oxford instruments) and ImageJ. Single nuclei were prepared from fresh frozen gut pieces as in ref. 87. Single-nuclei capture and sequencing were performed at the Cancer Genomics Platform of the Cancer Research Center of Lyon (CRCL). The gene expression matrices from Cell Ranger were used for downstream analysis using the software R and the R toolkit Seurat. Statistical tests were performed with Prism 9 using Mann–Whitney, chi2, or nonparametric ANOVA tests as stated in the figure legends.
